influences/incense-candles-processions/s: Incense offerings, lamps and torches carried before magistrates and emperors, and civic and agrarian processions
influences/incense-candles-processions/c: Liturgical censing, altar and processional lights, votive candles and litanies through the streets
influences/incense-candles-processions/e: The ceremonial use of lights and incense as marks of honour before a dignitary is well documented in late Roman court practice and plainly shaped papal and episcopal ritual. But incense and lamps also had deep Jewish and biblical roots, practical lamps were used from the start, and the earliest Christians explicitly refused pagan incense offerings. The result is a convergence rather than a simple borrowing.
influences/incense-candles-processions/p: Catholic and Orthodox incense, candles and processions are pagan temple rituals carried straight into the church.
influences/incense-candles-processions/w: For the first three centuries Christians rejected incense precisely because burning it before an image of the emperor or the gods was the test of apostasy (Pliny, Letters 10.96; the Decian libelli of 250). Incense enters Christian worship only after Constantine, first attested at the Jerusalem Anastasis by Egeria in the 380s, and it was justified from the Temple (Exodus 30), Malachi 1:11 and Revelation 5:8 and 8:3–4. Lamps were first practical (Acts 20:8) and then symbolic in the evening lucernarium, which echoed Jewish lamp-lighting blessings. What does come from the Roman state is the ceremonial of honour: lights and incense carried before high officials and the emperor were transferred to bishops and to the Gospel book, as Ordo Romanus I (c. 700) shows. Processions drew on both Roman civic pageantry and Jewish and biblical precedent, and in some cases (the Major Litany of 25 April) they replaced specific pagan rites.
influences/incense-candles-processions/s: Early Christians refused incense as an act of idolatry, but from the late fourth century incense, candles and processions became normal in worship. Their forms owe much to Roman court and civic ceremonial, their justification to the Temple and the Book of Revelation.

In the persecutions the line between Christian and pagan was drawn with a few grains of incense. Pliny the Younger tested accused Christians in Bithynia (c. 112) by making them offer incense and wine to the emperor’s image; in the Decian persecution of 250 certificates (libelli) recorded that the bearer had sacrificed. Tertullian (De idololatria 11) asked how a Christian incense seller could pass a temple ‘with a clear conscience’, and Athenagoras and Lactantius insisted that God needed no fragrant smoke. Pre-Constantinian Christian worship therefore had no liturgical incense, though incense was used at funerals to mask odour.

Lamps were another matter. Christians met at night and needed light (Acts 20:8), and the ritual lighting of the evening lamp — the lucernarium, with its ancient hymn Phos Hilaron, already called old by Basil of Caesarea (On the Holy Spirit 29.73) — echoed Jewish blessings over the lamp at the start of the Sabbath. Lights at tombs were more contentious: the Council of Elvira (c. 305, canon 34) forbade lighting candles in cemeteries by day ‘for the spirits of the saints must not be disturbed’, a sign that the custom was already popular and was felt to resemble pagan funerary practice.

After 312 the church moved into public buildings and absorbed public ceremonial. Lights and incense carried before a magistrate or emperor were insignia of rank in late Roman society; they were now carried before bishops, before the Gospel book and before the eucharistic gifts. Egeria, a pilgrim from the far West, describes censers brought into the Anastasis in Jerusalem at the Sunday vigil in the 380s so that ‘the whole basilica is filled with the smell’ (Itinerarium 24.10). By about 700 Ordo Romanus I has seven acolytes with candles and a subdeacon with a censer walking before the pope in the stational procession — an imperial-style entrance. Pseudo-Dionysius gave censing a mystical meaning as the divine fragrance going out to all and returning to its source.

Processions had both pagan and Jewish models. Rome’s litania maior on 25 April ran along the route once used for the Robigalia, the procession to protect crops from blight, and Gregory the Great organised the great sevenfold litany of 590 during plague; Rogation processions were introduced in Gaul by Bishop Mamertus of Vienne (c. 470). Defenders of candles, such as Jerome against Vigilantius (406), conceded that lights at martyrs’ tombs resembled pagan custom but argued that what was once done for idols was now done for God and his saints.

The Reformers largely removed these practices. Zwingli’s Zurich and Calvin’s Geneva abolished candles, incense and processions as unscriptural ceremonies; the Church of England kept some lights but banned most ceremony, and in the nineteenth-century ritualist controversies the Lincoln Judgment (1890) allowed altar candles while the Lambeth ‘Opinions’ of 1899 ruled ceremonial incense unlawful. Catholic, Orthodox and Oriental churches retain them, as do many Lutherans and Anglo-Catholics, and votive candles have spread even into some evangelical settings.

influences/saints-and-local-gods/sourceC: Local and healing deities, heroes and the Roman system of patronage (patronus and cliens)
influences/saints-and-local-gods/christi: The cult of saints as patrons and intercessors for cities, trades, illnesses and places
influences/saints-and-local-gods/evidenc: Specific substitutions are documented — healing shrines replacing Isis or Asclepius-style cults, churches placed on temples, saints taking over a god’s feast or function. But the wider thesis that the saints are simply pagan gods renamed is rejected by most historians since Peter Brown, who trace the cult of martyrs to Jewish and early Christian veneration of witnesses and to late Roman patronage. Scholars remain divided on how much continuity of popular religion there was.
influences/saints-and-local-gods/popular: The cult of the saints is polytheism in disguise: the old gods were given saints’ names, so St Brigid is the goddess Brigid, St George a sun-hero and the patron saints simply replaced the gods of trades and towns.
influences/saints-and-local-gods/whatHis: An older ‘history of religions’ school (Ernst Lucius, Pierre Saintyves’ Les saints successeurs des dieux, 1907) argued that saints succeeded the gods. The Bollandist Hippolyte Delehaye (The Legends of the Saints, 1905) accepted that some legends borrowed pagan motifs but showed that most saints were real Christians, usually martyrs with a fixed tomb and anniversary. Peter Brown’s The Cult of the Saints (1981) rejected the ‘two-tier’ model in which the church merely tolerated popular paganism: the cult of martyrs was led by bishops and elites and grew from Christian roots and from the Roman language of patronage and friendship. Real, local transfers did happen — the healing saints Cyrus and John at Menouthis, traditionally installed by Cyril of Alexandria to rival a shrine of Isis; Theodoret boasting that God had put his dead in the place of the gods — but these are instances of deliberate replacement, not proof that the saints were gods.
influences/saints-and-local-gods/summary: Christian saints became patrons and protectors of places, people and needs, often occupying the same shrines and functions as local gods and healing deities. How far this was continuity and how far conscious replacement is still debated.
influences/saints-and-local-gods/story:
The cult of the saints began with the martyrs. The Martyrdom of Polycarp (c. 155) records that the Smyrnaeans gathered his bones, ‘more precious than jewels’, to celebrate the ‘birthday’ of his martyrdom each year — a practice with precedent in Jewish honour for the tombs of prophets and martyrs (Matthew 23:29; the Maccabean martyrs). By the fourth century martyrs were invoked as intercessors, their shrines were the busiest places of Christian devotion, and their stories were read on their feast days.

The saints quickly took on the social role of patrons. In late Roman society a patronus protected, petitioned for and represented his clients; Paulinus of Nola addressed St Felix in exactly these terms, and cities acquired heavenly patrons — Ambrose at Milan, Martin at Tours, later Mark at Venice and Denis at Paris. Trades, illnesses and dangers acquired specialist saints in the Middle Ages, which is the strongest surface resemblance to the gods of the Roman pantheon.

Some cases are clear substitutions. Near Alexandria, the shrine of the healing saints Cyrus and John at Menouthis was traditionally founded by Cyril of Alexandria (c. 414) to draw pilgrims away from a famous shrine of Isis, and practised incubation — sleeping in the sanctuary for a healing dream — just as at the temples of Asclepius. Theodoret of Cyrrhus wrote (Cure of the Greek Maladies 8, c. 430s) that ‘the Lord has led his own dead into the temples in place of your gods’, and Gregory the Great’s letter to Mellitus (601) advised that English temples be rededicated to saints with feasts on the same days. In Ireland, St Brigid of Kildare shares a name and a feast (1 February, Imbolc) with a goddess, and Gerald of Wales (c. 1185) described a perpetual fire tended by nuns at Kildare, suggesting at least the absorption of older elements, although a historical Brigid is probable.

Other popular identifications fail. St George is a well-attested martyr cult from Lydda in Palestine; St Christopher’s legend is a Christian allegory; many supposed ‘gods in disguise’ were inferred only from similar names by nineteenth-century folklorists. The Catholic calendar reform of 1969 itself demoted saints of uncertain historicity such as Christopher, while keeping their cult locally.

The Reformers attacked the cult of saints as a denial of Christ’s sole mediation (Augsburg Confession, art. 21; Calvin, Institutes 3.20.21–27), and Protestant polemicists such as Conyers Middleton (Letter from Rome, 1729) argued that Roman Catholic devotion was pagan religion surviving under new names. Catholic and Orthodox theology answers with the distinction between latria (worship due to God alone) and dulia (honour given to saints), defined by the Second Council of Nicaea (787) and Trent (1563).
